title: Thyroid Function Patterns: TSH First, T3 Toxicosis, Graves and Iodine
summary: Read TSH, free T4 and T3 patterns, avoid the T3-toxicosis trap, separate Graves disease from toxic nodules with TSH-receptor antibodies and uptake scans, and keep the Wolff–Chaikoff and Jod-Basedow iodine effects straight.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 25 Hit 3 (TSH first-line; TSH/FT4/T3 patterns; T3 toxicosis), Hit 9 (Graves vs toxic nodule; TRAb; TPOAb), Hit 11 (Wolff–Chaikoff and Jod-Basedow) and Trap 2 (low TSH with normal FT4 and T3). Checked against Koulouri 2013, Sriphrapradang and Bhasipol 2016 (T3-toxicosis definition), Kahaly 2018 (ETA guideline; read via a page-fetch tool), Lee and Pearce 2023 (read via a page-fetch tool), Leung and Braverman 2014 (read via a page-fetch tool) and Klubo-Gwiezdzinska 2022 (read via a page-fetch tool). Qualified: Hit 11 phrasing “iodine deficiency → Jod-Basedow” (rv-jod-basedow-iodine-load); Hit 9 “TRAb/TSI positive in ~85%” (current assays ~97–98%; rv-trab-sensitivity); Hit 3 TSH alone misleads in central hypothyroidism and after treatment (rv-tsh-alone-limits). Not taught: the reviewer’s Number Vault TSH and total T4 reference intervals (method-dependent) and “Graves thyrotoxicosis: TSH <0.01”. The ATA 2016 hyperthyroidism guideline was not read. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) was blocked by a captcha and was not read.

objectives: Explain why TSH is the most sensitive first thyroid test and when TSH alone misleads.
Interpret TSH, free T4 and T3 patterns, including T3 toxicosis and subclinical hyperthyroidism.
Use TSH-receptor antibodies and uptake patterns to separate Graves disease, toxic nodules and low-uptake thyrotoxicosis.
Distinguish the Wolff–Chaikoff effect from the Jod-Basedow phenomenon.

scenes.title: Three low TSH results
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three thyroid panels, each with a low TSH. (1) A 34-year-old with palpitations: TSH undetectable, free T4 normal, T3 not yet measured. (2) A 29-year-old with a smooth goitre: TSH suppressed, free T4 high, TSH-receptor antibody pending. (3) A 76-year-old with a known multinodular goitre, three weeks after an iodinated-contrast CT: TSH suppressed, free T4 high. Question token: “Subclinical, Graves, or iodine?”

cues.text: Three thyroid panels, all with a low TSH. A young adult with palpitations has a normal free T4, and nobody has measured T3.
A second patient has a smooth goitre and a high free T4. A third, with a nodular goitre, became thyrotoxic weeks after an iodinated contrast scan.
Which one is not yet a diagnosis, which needs an antibody, and which was set off by iodine?

scenes.title: Why TSH goes first
scenes.altText: Schematic: hypothalamus–pituitary–thyroid loop. TSH and free T4 have an inverse log-linear relationship, so a small change in free T4 gives a large change in TSH; TSH is therefore the most sensitive single first test. Pattern cards: high TSH + low FT4 = primary hypothyroidism; low TSH + high FT4 and/or T3 = overt hyperthyroidism; low TSH + normal FT4 + normal T3 = subclinical hyperthyroidism. A warning card lists where TSH alone misleads: central (pituitary or hypothalamic) hypothyroidism, recent treatment of thyrotoxicosis, non-thyroidal illness, TSH assay interference, TSH-secreting adenoma, resistance to thyroid hormone.

cues.text: TSH goes first because of the shape of the feedback loop. TSH and free T4 have a log-linear relationship, so a small change in free T4 gives a large swing in TSH.
High TSH with low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism. Low TSH with high free T4 or T3 is overt hyperthyroidism.
Low TSH with a normal free T4 and a normal T3 is subclinical hyperthyroidism. Both hormones have to be measured before you can use that label.
TSH alone misleads when the pituitary is the problem, as in central hypothyroidism, and right after treatment of thyrotoxicosis, when TSH can stay low. That is why many labs pair TSH with free T4.

scenes.title: T3 toxicosis and the iodine switch
scenes.altText: Card 1: in milder hyperthyroidism free T4 can be normal while only T3 is high and TSH is undetectable (T3 toxicosis); measure T3 before calling it subclinical; total T3 may be preferred because free T3 assays are less accurate. Card 2, Wolff–Chaikoff: an acute iodine load transiently (about 24 h in the original rat work) reduces thyroid hormone synthesis; a normal gland escapes as sodium–iodide symporter expression falls; failure to escape (hypothyroidism) is a risk in autoimmune thyroid disease, previously treated Graves disease, and possibly fetuses and newborns. Card 3, Jod-Basedow: iodine-induced hyperthyroidism when an iodine load gives extra substrate to a susceptible gland — nodular goitre, latent Graves disease, long-standing iodine deficiency.

cues.text: Now the trap. In milder hyperthyroidism, free T4 can still be normal while only T3 is high and TSH is undetectable. That is T3 toxicosis, so measure T3 before calling a low TSH subclinical. Total T3 may be preferred, because free T3 assays are less accurate.
Iodine flips the switch both ways. In the Wolff–Chaikoff effect, a large iodine load briefly cuts thyroid hormone synthesis. A normal gland escapes as it takes up less iodide.
A damaged gland may fail to escape and become hypothyroid: autoimmune thyroid disease, previously treated Graves disease, and perhaps fetuses and newborns.
Jod-Basedow is the opposite: iodine-induced hyperthyroidism. The iodine load is extra raw material for a nodular goitre, latent Graves disease, or a gland used to long-standing iodine deficiency.

scenes.title: Finding the cause
scenes.altText: Cause cards. TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) are specific for Graves disease; current third-generation assays report about 97–98% sensitivity and about 98–99.5% specificity. Thyroid ultrasound with colour or power Doppler is the recommended imaging to support Graves disease; scintigraphy is suggested when nodules coexist with hyperthyroidism. Uptake patterns: diffusely increased = Graves; focally or heterogeneously increased (“hot” nodules) = toxic adenoma or toxic multinodular goitre; low or absent = thyroiditis, high iodine exposure, exogenous thyroid hormone. TPO antibodies mark Hashimoto thyroiditis (present in about 95%). Hook answers: (1) measure T3 — possible T3 toxicosis; (2) TRAb positive → Graves; (3) iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow) in a nodular goitre, expect low uptake.

cues.text: Once hyperthyroidism is confirmed, find the cause. TSH receptor antibodies are the Graves marker: current assays report sensitivity and specificity near ninety-seven percent or higher.

On scintigraphy, uptake is diffusely increased in Graves disease, focal or patchy over hot nodules in toxic nodular disease, and low after thyroiditis or a heavy iodine load. TPO antibodies, positive in about ninety-five percent, mark Hashimoto thyroiditis instead.
Back to the hook. Patient one needs a T3 before anyone says subclinical: this may be T3 toxicosis. Patient two, with a positive receptor antibody, has Graves disease.
Patient three has iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in a nodular goitre, Jod-Basedow, and the iodine load would make uptake low.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Low TSH + normal FT4 = subclinical hyperthyroidism” (✓ only if T3 is also normal; T3 toxicosis hides behind a normal FT4); “Iodine deficiency causes Jod-Basedow” (✓ Jod-Basedow is hyperthyroidism triggered by an iodine LOAD; long-standing deficiency is a risk factor); “Wolff–Chaikoff means iodine always causes hypothyroidism” (✓ the block is transient and a normal gland escapes; lasting hypothyroidism needs a susceptible gland).

cues.text: Trap one: low TSH with normal free T4 means subclinical. Only if T3 is normal too; T3 toxicosis hides behind a normal free T4.
Trap two: iodine deficiency causes Jod-Basedow. No: an iodine load causes it. Long-standing deficiency only makes the gland susceptible.
Trap three: Wolff–Chaikoff means iodine always causes hypothyroidism. No: the block is brief and a normal gland escapes.

props.title: ✗ “Iodine deficiency causes Jod-Basedow.”
lines: ✓ An iodine load does; deficiency = risk

scenes.title: Alarm, fire, fuel
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “TSH is the smoke alarm, T4 and T3 are the fire, iodine is the fuel. Check both flames before you call it a small fire. A flood of fuel briefly smothers a healthy furnace (Wolff–Chaikoff) but makes a starved, nodular furnace blaze (Jod-Basedow).” Tokens: alarm = TSH · fire = FT4 + T3 · fuel = iodine. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: TSH is the smoke alarm, T4 and T3 are the fire, and iodine is the fuel. Check both flames before calling it a small fire. A flood of fuel briefly smothers a healthy furnace, but makes a starved, nodular furnace blaze.

Where it breaks: the alarm itself can be faulty, as in pituitary disease or right after treatment; susceptibility to iodine is a risk, not a certainty; and antibody and uptake results depend on the assay and the clinical picture.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Iodine susceptibility is a risk, not a rule

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “TSH first · read it with free T4 and T3 · T3 toxicosis hides behind a normal FT4”, “Iodine load: brief block in a healthy gland (Wolff–Chaikoff) · hyperthyroidism in a susceptible gland (Jod-Basedow)”.

cues.text: TSH is the most sensitive first thyroid test, but read it with free T4 and T3 because T3 toxicosis hides behind a normal free T4, and remember that an iodine load briefly blocks a healthy gland while it can push a nodular or iodine-deficient gland into hyperthyroidism.

props.label: TSH first · read with FT4 and T3 · T3 toxicosis hides
Iodine load: brief block (W–C) · hyper if susceptible (J–B)

explanation.what: Plain language: the pituitary watches thyroid hormone and turns TSH up or down, and it responds steeply, so a small hormone change gives a large TSH change. A low TSH means too much hormone somewhere, but you must look at both T4 and T3 to know how much. Iodine is the thyroid’s raw material: a sudden flood makes a healthy gland pause, but can make a nodular or iodine-starved gland overproduce. Scientific terms: thyrotropin (TSH), free thyroxine (FT4), triiodothyronine (T3), inverse log-linear TSH–FT4 relationship, T3 toxicosis, subclinical hyperthyroidism, TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb/TSI), thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOAb), radioiodine uptake and scintigraphy, Wolff–Chaikoff effect, escape, sodium–iodide symporter, Jod-Basedow phenomenon.
explanation.why: Because TSH responds steeply to small hormone changes, it detects mild dysfunction that free T4 can miss; but the same logic fails if the pituitary is diseased or has not recovered after treatment. In mild hyperthyroidism T3 can rise before T4. Iodine excess acutely inhibits hormone synthesis, and the normal gland adapts; an abnormal gland may not adapt, or may use the extra iodine to make more hormone.
explanation.measure: Primary hypothyroidism: TSH high, FT4 low. Overt hyperthyroidism: TSH suppressed, FT4 and/or T3 high. Subclinical hyperthyroidism: TSH low with normal FT4 AND normal T3. T3 toxicosis: TSH undetectable, FT4 normal, T3 high (total T3 may be preferred because free T3 assays are less accurate). TRAb (third-generation): about 97–98% sensitive and 98–99.5% specific for Graves disease. Uptake: diffuse increase (Graves), focal or heterogeneous increase (toxic adenoma or multinodular goitre), low or absent (thyroiditis, high iodine exposure, exogenous hormone). TPOAb: present in about 95% of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
explanation.differs: Subclinical hyperthyroidism vs T3 toxicosis (T3 normal vs high); Graves disease vs toxic nodular disease (TRAb and diffuse vs focal uptake); Wolff–Chaikoff (iodine load → transient block, hypothyroidism if no escape) vs Jod-Basedow (iodine load → hyperthyroidism in a susceptible gland).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the pattern of low TSH, normal FT4 and high T3; pick the test that confirms Graves disease; predict uptake after iodine exposure; or identify which iodine effect explains thyrotoxicosis after contrast in an older patient with a nodular goitre.

comparisons.title: Wolff–Chaikoff vs Jod-Basedow

left.label: Wolff–Chaikoff
points: Hypothyroidism only if the gland fails to escape

right.label: Jod-Basedow
points: Nodular goitre, latent Graves, prior iodine deficiency

comparisons.distinguisher: Same trigger (an iodine load); opposite outcome, set by the gland’s susceptibility.

mnemonic.text: TSH is the smoke alarm, T4 and T3 are the fire, iodine is the fuel. Check both flames before you call it a small fire. A flood of fuel briefly smothers a healthy furnace (Wolff–Chaikoff) but makes a starved, nodular furnace blaze (Jod-Basedow).
mnemonic.explanation: Links TSH-first testing, the need for both FT4 and T3, and the two opposite iodine effects.
mnemonic.limitation: The alarm can be faulty (central hypothyroidism, recently treated thyrotoxicosis); iodine susceptibility is a risk, not a certainty; antibody and uptake results depend on the assay and clinical context.

questions.stem: A patient with palpitations has an undetectable TSH, a normal free T4 and a markedly raised total T3. What is the best interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. Suppressed TSH with normal free T4 and high T3 is T3-predominant hyperthyroidism.
Incorrect. Subclinical hyperthyroidism requires a normal T3 as well as a normal free T4.
Incorrect. Primary hypothyroidism shows a high TSH with a low free T4.
Incorrect. Central hypothyroidism is thyroid hormone deficiency from hypothalamic or pituitary disease, so it does not fit a high T3 with palpitations.

questions.stem: Three weeks after an iodinated-contrast CT, a 76-year-old with a long-standing multinodular goitre has a suppressed TSH and a high free T4. Which term fits best?

options.rationale: Correct. An iodine load can drive hyperthyroidism in a susceptible gland such as a nodular goitre.
Incorrect. The Wolff–Chaikoff effect is a transient decrease in hormone synthesis after an iodine load, not hyperthyroidism.

options.text: Failure to escape from the Wolff–Chaikoff effect
options.rationale: Incorrect. Failure to escape causes hypothyroidism, not a high free T4.
Incorrect. Free T4 is high, so this is overt thyrotoxicosis.

questions.stem: In a patient with confirmed hyperthyroidism, which finding most supports Graves disease rather than a toxic adenoma?

options.text: Positive TSH-receptor antibody with diffusely increased uptake
options.rationale: Correct. TRAb is the Graves-specific marker, and uptake is diffusely increased in Graves disease.

options.text: Focally increased uptake in a single nodule
options.rationale: Incorrect. A focal “hot” nodule points to a toxic adenoma.
Incorrect. Low uptake suggests thyroiditis, a heavy iodine load or exogenous hormone.
Incorrect. TPO antibodies are the characteristic marker of Hashimoto thyroiditis (about 95% positive); TRAb is the Graves-specific test.

claims.text: TSH is the most sensitive first test because of the log-linear TSH–FT4 relationship; basic TSH/FT4 patterns; conditions where TSH alone misleads.
Subclinical hyperthyroidism needs normal FT4 and T3; T3-predominant disease with normal FT4 and undetectable TSH; total T3 may be preferred.
claims.note: Kahaly 2018 describes the pattern (only free T3 raised, undetectable TSH) without the term “T3 toxicosis”; Sriphrapradang and Bhasipol 2016 define T3-toxicosis as high T3 and low TSH with a normal T4. Lee and Pearce 2023 do not use the term.

claims.text: Wolff–Chaikoff transient block, escape and failure to escape; Jod-Basedow iodine-induced hyperthyroidism and its risk factors.
TRAb performance; ultrasound and scintigraphy roles; uptake patterns for Graves, toxic nodules and low-uptake causes.
TPO antibodies present in about 95% of Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Scenario invented; loop and uptake drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 25 Hit 11 says “iodine deficiency → Jod-Basedow phenomenon (hyperthyroidism)” and “iodine excess … (hypothyroidism)”. Leung and Braverman 2014 describe Jod-Basedow as hyperthyroidism induced by an iodine LOAD, with long-standing iodine deficiency, nodular goitre and latent Graves disease as risk factors; the Wolff–Chaikoff block is transient and normal glands escape, while hypothyroidism develops in susceptible glands that fail to escape. The lesson teaches the source (register flag rv-jod-basedow-iodine-load).

Ch. 25 Hit 9 gives TRAb/TSI as positive in “~85% of Graves”. Kahaly 2018 (pooled 97% sensitivity, 98% specificity) and Lee and Pearce 2023 (third-generation assays 97.7% / 99.5%) report higher figures for current assays; sensitivity is assay-generation dependent. The lesson uses ~97–98% (register flag rv-trab-sensitivity).

Ch. 25 Hit 3 presents TSH as the first-line test without its limits. Koulouri 2013 lists conditions in which TSH alone misleads (central hypothyroidism, recently treated thyrotoxicosis, non-thyroidal illness, assay interference, TSHoma, resistance to thyroid hormone), and Kahaly 2018 notes accuracy improves when TSH and free T4 are measured together. The lesson adds these limits (register flag rv-tsh-alone-limits).
